stories.title: Showcase: Climate Adaptation in Canada
stories.description: Key ways in which earth observation can inform climate adaptation efforts across Canada.

content.title: ESA and Canada
content.description:
The [European Space Agency](www.esa.int) (ESA) is a world-leader in Earth observation. It provides cutting-edge space data from its fleet of satellites, while supporting efforts to use this data to help understand the planet, to improve daily lives, benefit businesses and the economy, and to support effective policy-making for a more sustainable future. 

ESA also supports the European Commission in the implementation of the [Copernicus programme](https://eu-space.europa.eu/earth-observation).

Canada has a [cooperation agreement](https://www.asc-csa.gc.ca/eng/funding-programs/canada-esa/about-cooperation-agreement.asp) with ESA, allowing Canadian industry and researchers to participate in select ESA programs, and allowing Canadian stakeholders to benefit from the outputs of the user-oriented projects that ESA fund.

In this presentation we showcase some of the outputs of ESA's projects and tools most relevant to climate adaptation.

content.title: A changing climate
content.description:
Satellite data records stretch back to the 1970s, giving a long baseline to assess changes and estimate future trends.

Such data has been critical in the study of deforestation, ice loss, sea level trends and GHG emissions, among many others. It also provides key inputs to models of future climate behaviour.

![Canada temperature over time](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f5/Show_Your_Stripes_change_in_temperature_graphic_for_All_of_Canada_with_bars.png?utm_source=commons.wikimedia.org&utm_campaign=index&utm_content=original)
*Image credits: Professor Ed Hawkins, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons*

This image shows the land cover of Canada in 2021, as mapped by the [ESA WorldCover](https://esa-worldcover.org/en) project. Looking at land cover over time is the basis for many further applications.

content.title: Expanding cities
content.description:
Long term satellite measurements can show the growth of cities over time, showing the pressure that tbey put on the neighbouring environemnt..

This image shows the expansion of the city of Edmonton from 1985 to 2019, Redder areas have been there the longest, while blue and black pixels show more recent developments.

![Edmonton, Alberta](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/fc/Edmonton_downtown_in_winter%2C_2025%2C_Alberta%2C_Canada1.jpg?utm_source=commons.wikimedia.org&utm_campaign=index&utm_content=original)
*Image credits: Joli Rumi, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons*

content.title: Urban Heat Islands
content.description:
Increasing heat is one of the deadliest effects of climate change. Within cities the [urban heat island](https://climateatlas.ca/urban-heat-island-effect) effect amplifies the effects of rising heat. Satellites can help monitor the development of heat islands over time, providing cities with actionable information on where to focus their efforts.

This image shows the Land Surface Temperature in Vancouver, BC, on 25 June 2021, in the middle of the [deadliest heat dome effect](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/2021-bc-heat-dome-look-back-five-years-later-9.7246604) in Canadian history. 

This measurement was taken by the NASA ECOSTRESS instrument mounted aboard the International Space Station.

![ECOSTRESS on ISS](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/9f/Ecostress_on_ISS_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=commons.wikimedia.org&utm_campaign=index&utm_content=original)

*Image: NASA/JPL-Caltech, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons*

content.title: Urban Greening
content.description:
Trees and green spaces help to reduce extreme heat through shade and evapotranspiration. A common climate adaptation measure is to increase the greenness of a city.

As part of its [climate plan](https://montreal.ca/en/articles/greening-montreal-to-adapt-to-climate-change), the city of Montreal is aiming to plant 50,000 trees, prioritising those areas most vulnerable to heat island effects.

Satellite data are widely used to monitor the extent and health of urban vegetation. This map shows the [NDVI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normalized_difference_vegetation_index), a commonly used index for looking at vegetation, averaged over the year 2021.

![A Montreal Street](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/a6/2016-10_Montreal_41.jpg?utm_source=commons.wikimedia.org&utm_campaign=index&utm_content=original)
*Image credits: 0x010C, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons*

content.title: Wildfires
content.description:
As the climate gets hotter and drier, wildfires become more frequent and more dangerous. Satellites have a critical role in the early detection of wildfires; their high vantage point allows them to monitor wide areas, while their ability to see infra-red wavelengths allos them to directly detect the heat signature of a fire.

This image was taken by Sentinel-2 on 14th July 2026, and shows the plumes of smoke coming from wildfires in northern Ontario. The image has been enhanced to emphasise the smoke and burned area (red pixels).

![Wildfire in 2016](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f3/Landscape_view_of_wildfire_near_Highway_63_in_south_Fort_McMurray.jpg?utm_source=commons.wikimedia.org&utm_campaign=index&utm_content=original)
*Image Credits: DarrenRD, CC by 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons*

content.title: Air quality
content.description:
As well as directly threatening populated areas, smoke from wildfires can travel long distances. Particles from this smoke can have a range of effects including causing severe asthma attacks. Some satellites are able to track such atmospheric emissions. 

This map shows the total aerosol density over North America on 15th July 2026, at the peak of the wildfire season, as measured by the Sentinel-5P spacecraft. The image below shows how the sky looked form Toronto that day.

![Orange sky in Toronto](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/bc/Toronto_wildfire_smoke_July_15%2C_2026.jpg?utm_source=commons.wikimedia.org&utm_campaign=index&utm_content=original)
*Image Credits: ARandomName123, [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0), via Wikimedia Commons*

content.title: Arctic Regions
content.description:
Rising temperatures cause a different set of problems in arctic regions, as melting permafrost undermines the foundations of buildings, roads and railways, while increasing the risks of landslides and floods. Wildlife patterns also change as the weather warms, leading to loss of fishing resources and a higher risk of bear encounters.

Satellites can be used to monitor key infrastructure for subsidence and other damage, as well as looking for warning signs such as increased melting. This images shows a Sentinel-2 image of melting snow around Churchill, Manitoba, on 15th June 2026. 

![Polar bear statue](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/95/Churchill_polar_bear_statue.JPG?utm_source=commons.wikimedia.org&utm_campaign=index&utm_content=original)
*Image credits: Ian Stewart, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons*

content.title: Meanwhile across the Atlantic...
content.description:
The challenges faced by Canadian cities are not unique, but are faced by many cities worldwide. ESA has been supporting European companies to build EO-based services that can support climate adaptation efforts.

The [Stakeholder Engagement Facility](www.esa-sef.eu) has been with a range of European cities to help them incorporate such services into their daily work. Further resources can be found on the [SEF's urban page](https://sef.apex.esa.int/en/key-themes/urban-areas).

For more information on available services, see the other showcases on this site, or visit the SEF's [Urban Service Catalogue](https://sef.apex.esa.int/en/what-we-do/training/urban-eo-services-catalogue).

More information on how satellites benefit Canadians can be found on the [Canadian Space Agency](https://www.asc-csa.gc.ca/eng/satellites/everyday-lives/) website.

stories.title: Showcase: EO for Climate Adaptation
stories.description: Exploring the different ways that EO is used to support climate adaptation efforts within Europe.

content.title: Introduction
content.description:
Europe's climate is changing fast. Heatwaves, droughts, floods and other extreme weather events are becoming more frequent and more severe, and Europe's cities and regions need to adapt.

Satellite Earth Observation is a key resource in climate adaptation, providing early warnings, monitoring adaptation efforts, and supporting future predictions. Cities are increasingly using such tools to inform their planning.

This image shows the land surface temperature measured by the Sentinel-3 spacecraft in the last 10 days of July 2026.

content.title: Bordeaux: Urban Mapping
content.description:
Accurate knowledge of the city landscapes is essential to support planning decisions. The [Copernicus Land Monitoring Service](https://land.copernicus.eu/en) produces regular maps of land cover within Europe. 

The [CLMS Urban Atlas](https://land.copernicus.eu/en/products/urban-atlas), shown here for the city of Bordeaux, uses a combination of different types of satellite data, together with arial surveys and in-situ data, to give detailed assessment of Land Cover and Land Use in urban areas across Europe. 

Such data can be used to support planning decisions, but also for reporting cities commitments under legislation, for example assessing the fraction of a city dedicated to public green areas.

![Bordeaux](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/9f/Place_de_la_Bourse_Bordeaux_de_nuit.jpg?utm_source=commons.wikimedia.org&utm_campaign=index&utm_content=original)
*Image: Fabien1309, CC BY-SA 2.0 FR, via Wikimedia Commons*

content.title: Milan: Tree Cover
content.description:
The CLMS also produces regular maps of [street trees](https://land.copernicus.eu/en/products/urban-atlas?tab=street_tree_layer) in cities across Europe.

This images shows the tree cover from CLMS superimposed on a map of Land Surface Temperature provided by [ConstellR](https://www.constellr.com/). Tree cover is shown in green, while red and blue indicated hotter and cooler areas. The correlation between tree cover and urban heat can be clearly seen.

![Milan Park](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/62/Milano_-_platano_comune_-_id_03F20505F205MI03_%282%29.jpg?utm_source=commons.wikimedia.org&utm_campaign=index&utm_content=original)
*Image: Ysogo, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons*

content.title: Vienna: building footprints
content.description:
Although useful, the CLMS services have some limitations in terms of timeliness and resolution. There are several services available which provide frequent and detailed maps of key information such as building construction, green areas or PV installation.

This image shows building footprints in Modling, a suburb of Vienna. White footprints show buildings present in 2017, while red buildings were constructed between 2017 and 2025. The redder the building, the more recently it was constructed. 

This service was developed by (UblCube)[https://www.ubicube.eu/] in the framework of the [GTIF Austria](https://gtif-austria.info/) project.

Such services can also be used as the starting point for further analysis, for example to identify brownfield sites for development or to combine with heat maps to estimate building efficiency.

content.title: Copenhagen: Green Infrastructure
content.description:
Many cities have targets for reducing their carbon footprint, and installing solar photovoltaic (PV) panels can be an effective way to do this.

This image shows a mapping of PV panels (in yellow) in Copenhagen, using an [online service](https://algorithm-catalogue.apex.esa.int/apps/solar_pv_detection#execution-information) which detects ground-mounted and rooftop solar PV panels from Sentinel-2 L1C imagery using a deep-learning segmentation model. 

The service is openly available through [ESA's APEx platform](https://apex.esa.int/).

![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/ff/Copenhagen_International_School_%28solar_fa%C3%A7ade%29.jpg?utm_source=commons.wikimedia.org&utm_campaign=index&utm_content=original)
*Image: Solar Facade on the Copenhagen International School. *
*Credit: Marta Victoria, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.*

content.title: Vilnius: Urban heat trends
content.description:
Increasing temperatures are a major problem for cities, exacerbated by the [Urban Heat island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_heat_island) effect. Several EO-based tools are being developed to look at urban heat, both to provide detailed maps of past temperatures and to forecast future trends, aiming to identify areas where specific action is needed.

This example, from the ESA-funded [GTIF Baltic](https://gtif-baltic.info/story/?id=UHTM_01) project, shows the mean LST in Vilnius. The service fuses several data sources to estimate trends at the level of municipal districts.

![GTIF Dashboard](https://sef-prod-public.obs.eu-nl.otc.t-systems.com/urban/Europe_showcase/GTIF%20Baltic%20heat%20trend%20service.png)

content.title: Warsaw: Air quality
content.description:
Heat is not the only challenge facing cities. Air quality is also a major concern, as this can lead to respiratory illnesses and other health issues. 

Satellites measure pollutants over a wide area, but with some limitations, for example they often measure pollution throughout the atmosphere and not near ground level. However measurements from satellites can be combined with models and in-situ sensors to produce a more detailed map and forecast of street level air quality. 

This image shows an example of how satellite measurements of nitrogen dioxide have been downscales to give more detailed forecasts for the city of Warsaw. 

Such data can be included directly into street level forecasts: [click here](https://explore.lobelia.earth/citysatair) for an example.

This work was performed as part of the ESA-funded CitySatAir[](https://citysatair.nilu.no/) project.

content.title: Valencia: Flood Risk
content.description:
The city of Valencia in Spain was badly hit by floods in 2024. Satellites have a key role in responding to disasters such as floods, but can also support preparation efforts.

This image shows flood hazard models from the [Copernicus Emergency Management Service](https://emergency.copernicus.eu/use-cases/floods-early-warning-and-monitoring/). These incorporate accurate [Digital Elevation Models](https://dataspace.copernicus.eu/explore-data/data-collections/copernicus-contributing-missions/collections-description/COP-DEM) from satellite data. CEMS also uses a range of satellite inputs to provide early warning of flood conditions.

![CEMS bulletin](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c1/The_Copernicus_Emergency_Management_Service_monitors_the_floods_in_Valencia%2C_Spain_%28Copernicus_2024-11-03%29.png?utm_source=commons.wikimedia.org&utm_campaign=index&utm_content=original)
*Image: Copernicus Emergency Management Service. Contains modified Sentinel data.*

content.title: Bregenz: Infrastructure Monitoring
content.description:
Synthetic Aperture Radar satellites, such as Sentinel-1, bounce microwaves off the Earth's surface to create high-resolution images, regardless of cloud or daylight. Combining SAR images from different times allows small changes in the earth's surface to be seen. This is useful for monitoring deformations in the Earth's surface which can impact buildings or infrastructure.

This example shows deformation monitoring of the E60 motorway near Bregenz, Austria. It uses [a service](https://gtif-austria.info/narratives/monitoring_transport_infrastructure) developed by the Austrian Institute of Technology in the framework of the [GTIF Austria](https://gtif-austria.info/) project.

![Bregenz Motorway](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/2e/Bregenz-motorway_entrance_Weidach-01ESD.jpg?utm_source=commons.wikimedia.org&utm_campaign=index&utm_content=original)
*Image: Rikki Mitterer, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons*

content.title: Conclusion
content.description:
The examples presented here are just some of the services available to European cities to support climate adaptation planning. There are many others, some of which are free and open, while others are paid commercial services. Some are developed for a specific city or country, others are widely available.

The [Stakeholder Engagement Facility](www.esa-sef.eu) has been with a range of European cities to understand their needs and to help them incorporate such services into their daily work. We encourage cities to [contact us](https://esa-sef.eu/contact/) to discuss their circumstances.

Further resources can be found on the [SEF's urban page](https://sef.apex.esa.int/en/key-themes/urban-areas).

For more information on available services, see the other stories on this site, or visit the SEF's [Urban Service Catalogue](https://sef.apex.esa.int/en/what-we-do/training/urban-eo-services-catalogue).

stories.title: Toronto: Air Quality from Wildfires
stories.description: The impact of the 2025 wildfires on air quality in Toronto

content.title: Introduction
content.description:
As the climate warms, Canada is experiencing longer wildfire seasons and more frequent wildfires. As well as the immediate damage caused, wildfire smoke can travel long distances from the actual fire, causing problems to many urban regions.

Satellite data have a key role to play at all stages: they give key inputs to forecasting (such as measurements of temperature and soil moisture), they are critical for the early detection of wildfires, and they can support in assessing their impacts.

Operational services, such as the [Canadian Wildland Fire Information System ](https://cwfis.cfs.nrcan.gc.ca/en) use satellite data as the basis for warnings. 

This image shows [current active fires](https://cwfis.cfs.nrcan.gc.ca/en/interactive-map?layerIds=public%3Acwfif_national_activefires&selectedDate=2026-07-29&center=-87.1_47.9&zoom=1.11) as monitored by CWFIS.

content.title: Detecting wildfires from space
content.description:
Satellites have a critical role in the early detection of wildfires; their high vantage point allows them to monitor wide areas, while their ability to see infra-red wavelengths allos them to directly detect the heat signature of a fire.

This image was taken by Sentinel-2 on 14th July 2026, and shows the plumes of smoke coming from wildfires in northern Ontario. The image has been enhanced to emphasise the smoke and burned area (red pixels).

content.title: Wildfires on 15th July 2026
content.description:
Bringing together such data from a wide range of satellites allows us to see the situation across a wide territory. 

This images shows thermal anomalies (i.e. likely wildfires) detected by NASA's [MODIS](https://modis.gsfc.nasa.gov/) instruments on 15th July 2026, at the height of the wildfire season.

content.title: Wildfire smoke
content.description:
As well as the wildfires themselves, satellites also monitor the progress of the smoke plume. 

This images uses [Aerosol Optical Depth](https://www.earthdata.nasa.gov/topics/atmosphere/aerosol-optical-depth-thickness), as measured by the [Sentinel-5P](https://www.esa.int/Applications/Observing_the_Earth/Copernicus/Sentinel-5P), to track the progress of the smoke plume.

Use the time controls to see the evolution of the smoke plume.

content.title: Air quality in Toronto
content.description:
Smoke can cause problems in cities from the source. Wildfire smoke has a range of [health impacts](https://www.canada.ca/en/services/health/healthy-living/environment/air-quality/wildfire-smoke/health-effects-exposure.html) ranging from minor headaches to severe asthma.

This image shows the same Aerosol Optical Depth](https://www.earthdata.nasa.gov/topics/atmosphere/aerosol-optical-depth-thickness) from [Sentinel-5P](https://www.esa.int/Applications/Observing_the_Earth/Copernicus/Sentinel-5P) as before, but zoomed in (and made partially transparent) to show the effects in Toronto and neighbouring ciites.
.
Use the time controls to see the evolution of the smoke plume.

content.title: A hazy day in the city
content.description:
The effects of the smoke are clearly visible in this Sentinel-2 image, taken on 16th July 2026, in which the city of Toronto is partly hidden under this cloud.

The image below (taken on 15th July) shows how this looks at the ground level, with the sky taking on an orange colour.

![Orange sky in Toronto](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/bc/Toronto_wildfire_smoke_July_15%2C_2026.jpg?utm_source=commons.wikimedia.org&utm_campaign=index&utm_content=original)
*Image Credits: ARandomName123, [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0), via Wikimedia Commons*

content.title: Heat stress and air quality
content.description:
By nature, wildfires tend to happen more frequently in hot, dry periods. Since cities typically tend to be slightly hotter than surrounding areas (the [Urban Heat Island](https://climateatlas.ca/urban-heat-island-effect) effect), this means that heat stress and poor air quality often come together, which can be dangerous to people with poor health.

This image (from NASA's [ECOSTRESS](https://ecostress.jpl.nasa.gov/) instrument) shows the land surface temperature (in Kelvin) on 14th July 2026. Although LST is not the temperature that people experience directly it is a reasonable proxy.

content.title: Conclusion
content.description:
## Further Reading

[Toronto Wildfire Smoke Strategy.](https://www.toronto.ca/community-people/health-wellness-care/health-programs-advice/air-quality/wildfire-air-quality-strategy/)

## News Articles

[The deadly health burden of wildfire smoke.](https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-interactive/2026/aug/08/wildfire-smoke-unknown-health-impacts)(The Guardian, 8th August 2026)

stories.title: Rotterdam Flood Protection
stories.description: Supporting flood prevention in the Netherlands

content.title: Introduction
content.description:
Rotterdam is the second-largest city in the Netherlands, wth approximately 674 thousand residents. It is a major economic hub; The port of Rotterdam is Europe's largest, with around 28,000 ships arriving each year. 

Rotterdam faces similar climate challenges to those faced by other European cites, such as increasing heat and drought, but it also faces specific challenges as a result of its location.

![Rotterdam Panorama](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f8/Erasmusbrug_seen_from_Euromast.jpg?utm_source=commons.wikimedia.org&utm_campaign=index&utm_content=original)
*Image: Mlefter, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons*

content.title: Topography
content.description:
Like many parts of the Netherlands, Rotterdam sits largely below sea level. About 85% of the city is below sea level, in some cases by up to 7m.

This image shows the [Copernicus Digital Elevation Model](https://dataspace.copernicus.eu/explore-data/data-collections/copernicus-contributing-missions/collections-description/COP-DEM), based on data collected by the German [TANDEM-X](https://earth.esa.int/eogateway/missions/terrasar-x-and-tandem-x) spacecraft. 

Dark blue areas show the lowest areas, light blue shows areas which are higher (but still below sea level).

content.title: Flood risk
content.description:
This DEM, as well as other parameters (such as the level of protection) can be used to build models showing where the risk of flooding is highest.

This model comes from the [Copernicus Emergency Management Service](https://emergency.copernicus.eu/), with areas considered to be at higher risk of flooding shown in a darker shade of blue.

content.title: Impact Assessment
content.description:
Satellite data also have a role to play in assessing the impact of any floods. This image shows the [CLMS Urban Atlas](https://land.copernicus.eu/en/products/urban-atlas) product, which uses satellite, airborne and in-situ data to determine composition of European cities.

Comparing such a map to the flood risk allows an indication of the potential damage from a flood event.

content.title: Flood protection
content.description:
Satellite data are also used to actively determine when protection measures are needed.

The Netherlands is protected by a series of flood prevention measures known as the [Delta Works](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delta_Works). One of the most famous components of this are the [Maeslantkering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maeslantkering), shown below and on the right (Sentinel-2 image).

![Maeslantkering](
https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/af/Maeslantkering.jpg?utm_source=commons.wikimedia.org&utm_campaign=index&utm_content=original)

*Image credits: DeltaWorks Online - Eszter Simonfi, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons*

content.title: Forecasting floods
content.description:
Satellite data are used to monitor conditions in the North sea to determine when these gates need to be closed to prevent a [storm surge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storm_surge) entering the river.

Sea heights are measured continuously using a combination of tide gauges and satellite data (altimeters). These are fed into a model along with other data, including the weather forecast, to predict when a high sea level is due at Rotterdam.

 This images shows sea level anomaly (i.e. height above that expected) as provided by the [Copernicus Marine Service](https://marine.copernicus.eu/).

content.title: Conclusion
content.description:
Space based data had a critical role to play in both planning and responding to floods. By using such data effectively cities such as Rotterdam can improve their response to sea level rise and a changing climate.

## Further Reading

[Rotterdam Climate Adaptation Strategy](https://www.urbanisten.nl/work/rotterdam-adaptation-strategy)

[C40 Cities: Rotterdam](https://www.c40.org/case-studies/c40-good-practice-guides-rotterdam-climate-change-adaptation-strategy/)

stories.title: Marseille Urban Heat
stories.description: Urban heat in the city of Marseille

content.title: Introduction
content.description:
The most populated city in the south of France, Marseille is increasingly affected by rising temperatures. In 2026 there were three consecutive heatwaves, with a peak temperature of 38.1 C recorded on 5 July.

To cope with a changing climate, Marseille has been looking at how it can [adapt its public spaces](https://eu-mayors.ec.europa.eu/en/%20Refreshing-Marseille-with-cooler-greener-and-accessible-public-spaces) to become greener and cooler.

This composite Sentinel-1 image shows Marseille and the surrounding areas, including the [Calenques National Park](https://www.calanques-parcnational.fr/en) South of the main city.

content.title: Looking beyond the visible
content.description:
Satellites can detect a wider range of wavelengths than the human eye. This Sentinel-2 image shows Marseille in near-infrared (NIR). In this wavelength vegetation is easily seen (darker red), while buildings and other artificial surfaces show up in grey.

NIR measurements (with a wavelength of about 840nm) do not show heat directly, For this we need to instead look at **thermal infrared**, with a wavelength of several micrometers.

content.title: Land Surface Temperature
content.description:
This image shows the **Land Surface Temperature** over Marseille, taking a ten day average, as measured by the SLSTR instrument on board the Sentinel-3 spacecraft. 

Land surface temperature is not necessarily the temperature that people will experience (air temperatures) but is a reasonably close proxy.

This image shows for the last 10 days of June 2026, during the first heatwave of the year. Use the calendar tool to change date and see how the heatwave evolved.

The resolution of the SLSTR instrument is approximately 1km, which is good enough to see broad-brush features (such as the magnitude of the urban heat islands effect), but not to look at individual streets or buildings.

content.title: Higher Resolution LST Measurements
content.description:
For more detailed (and more frequent) measurements of temperature, various commercial data are available.

This image, provide by the German satellite company [Constellr](https://www.constellr.com/), shows LST over Marseille at a 30m resolution.

content.title: Street level comparison
content.description:
At 30m resolution, it is possible to see heat island effects at the individual building scale.

This image compares the 30m heat map from Constellr with [OpenStreetMap](https://openstreetmap.org) information to help locate specific hotspots, such as the one shown here close to the main train station.

content.title: Heat islands and urban green
content.description:
We can also overlay data showing the presence of [street trees](https://land.copernicus.eu/en/products/urban-atlas?tab=street_tree_layer) (taken from the [Copernicus Urban Atlas](https://land.copernicus.eu/en/products/urban-atlas)).

Neighbourhoods with more trees are generally [significantly cooller](https://climate-adapt.eea.europa.eu/en/metadata/publications/urban-greening-cools-cities-and-saves-lives) than those without such vegetation, and the correlation can be seen in this area.

content.title: Night time temperatures
content.description:
We can also compare land surface temperatures at night. Redder areas indicate hotter temperatures.

Zooming out we can see that the urban areas retain their heat more than the surrounding countryside, meaning that city residents experience a higher night time temperature, which can significantly affect sleep patterns.

content.title: Conclusion
content.description:
A wide variety of tools exist to help cities map urban heat islands, model their future evolution, and devise strategies for dealing with them. Please [contact the SEF team](https://sef.apex.esa.int/en/contact-us) if you would like to discuss your specific needs.

stories.title: Vienna: green transition
stories.description: Providing actionable information supporting the green transition.

content.title: Introduction
content.description:
The city of Vienna aims to achieve climate neutrality by 2040 through its [Smart Climate City Strategy](https://smartcity.wien.gv.at/en/strategy/). 

To achieve this will require action in areas such as emissions reduction, expanding green spaces, and increasing sustainable mobility. This is a key part of the overall ambitious Green Transition strategy within Austria.

The [Green Transition Information Factory](http://gtif.esa.int) (GTIF) was an ESA initiative designed to demonstrate the ability of Earth Observation (EO), to provide actionable information in support of the Green Transition and the European Green Deal.

Austria served as the initial test bed for the GTIF concept, with several Austrian companies and organizations contributing under a strongly user-driven approach.

content.title: Urban Heat
content.description:
Like many European cities, Vienna is experiencing longer and more intense heatwaves. In 2026 temperatures reached a [record high of 41 C](https://www.euractiv.com/news/austria-breaks-heat-record-under-new-european-heat-dome/).

This image shows the Land Surface Temperatures (LST) over Austria in the period June 1st and June 24th for 3 years (2022-2024), as measured by the ECOSTRESS instrument mounted on the International Space Station.

Such inputs are used to build tools that monitor [urban heat trends](https://gtif-austria.info/narratives/urban-heat-trend-monitor), allowing urban hotspots to be detected, and to [forecast temperatures](https://gtif-austria.info/narratives/temperature-forecast) to prioritise actions.

content.title: Dynamic building footprints
content.description:
The starting point for urban planning is to have a clear picture of what is present. Satellite data can give frequent updates of buildings, allowing rapid detection of new construction.

This images shows example data from the [GTIF Building Footprints service](https://gtif-austria.info/narratives/building_footprints), showing buildings in the Modling suburb of Vienna. 

Building in white were already present in 2017, while those in pink or red were constructed between 2017 and 2025. The redder the footprint, the more recently it was constructed.

This service was developed by ubicube GmbH.

content.title: Urban Energy Performance Monitor
content.description:
Improving the energy efficiency of buildings serves to reduce energy use.

The EU [Energy Performance of Buildings Directive](https://energy.ec.europa.eu/topics/energy-efficiency/energy-performance-buildings/energy-performance-buildings-directive_en) sets targets for both residential and non-residential buildings.

Energy efficiency can be estimated from satellite data by looking at the effective temperature difference between remotely observed temperature and global temperature, assuming normal building usage and sufficient contrast between outdoor and indoor temperature (e.g. comparison in winter conditions).

This image shows an Urban Energy Performance Index (UEPI) combining localised heat loss signals from LST analysis, building age, and building size into a prioritisation for retrofitting. Buildings marked in red have been assessed as being less energy efficient, buildings in green more efficient.

content.title: Brownfield potential
content.description:
To promote sustainable building development, reuse of existing sites—so-called brownfields—is an essential strategy. Such sites offer several advantages, as they are often already integrated into local supply networks, benefit from established infrastructure, and are easily accessible for employees.

Within the GTIF Austria initiative a tool has been developed which uses A) and remote sensing data to identify sealed, underutilized surfaces, assigning each plot a probability score. This supports cities in prioritising areas for land recycling.

This tool was developed by the Environment Agency Austria (Umweltbundesamt) in collaboration with Fraunhofer IIS.

content.title: Rooftop characterisation
content.description:
The efficient use of roofs can support the green transition. Installing green roofs can provide shade in summer and insulation in winter, reducing building energy use. Alternatively a roof may be used to generate renewable energy through PhotoVoltaic panels. 

This image shows the outputs of a service for mapping rooftop use, developed by N-Vision. It provides efficient and accurate mapping of solar panel installations and of green roofs by analysing satellite or aerial imagery using state-of-the-art computer vision methods.

Green roofs are shown in green, PV installations in green.

content.title: Conclusion
content.description:
The services developed under the [GTIF Austria](https://gtif-austria.info/) activity have shown how such services can develop into a sustainable operational framework meeting national needs.

As well as the urban services showcased here, the GTIF has also developed other tools, for example for estimating the potential energy from solar installations, as shown in this image.

Other GTIF instances are under development, covering different themes and different areas of Europe. Such projects aim to tackle the “last kilometer” challenge, bridging the gap between EO capability development and the operational uptake.

For more information on GTIF or other urban services, please contact the ESA [Stakeholder Engagement Facility](www.esa-sef.eu) team.

The Building Footprints service combines advanced satellite imagery analysis with sophisticated data processing to provide accurate, timely information about urban development and infrastructure changes. This service delivers up-to-date, spatially and temporally consistent building data, serving as a fundamental component for Smart City solutions.

So called "brownfield" sites offer several advantages for urban development, as they are often already integrated into local supply networks, benefit from established infrastructure, and are easily accessible for employees.

The Brownfield Recovery Potential (BRP) Interactive Map is a geospatial web based tool designed to identify and analyze underutilized commercial sites (brownfields) across Austria. This initiative aligns with Austria’s sustainability policies by promoting the redevelopment of brownfields instead of increasing urban sprawl.

Developed as a free and open service by Umweltbundesamt (UBA) Austria’s Federal Environment Agency, in collaboration with Fraunhofer IIS, the BRP map identifies approximately 5,700 commercial locations exceeding 1,000 m², making them prime candidates for redevelopment.

UEPI (Urban Energy Performance Index) combines heat‑loss signals (from LST analysis), building age, and building size into a relative retrofit‑priority score.
Scale 0–100: 0 = high retrofit need (high priority), 100 = good (low priority).
Weighting: heat loss 50%, age 30%, size 20%. Critical cases (high loss + old building) and very large buildings receive additional amplification.
